introduction: These are ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s memories of May 1892 and the years after: his father handing him the papers, “the Supreme Affliction”, the night when sorrows intensified, enemies within and without, and then letter after letter telling the bereaved that the Light shines on from another horizon and that rest is forbidden while the work remains. Every community that has lost its founder has had such days. Elisha cries “My father, my father”; Israel loses Moses at the border; the disciples hear that it is expedient for them that he go, and stand gazing after him; Paul warns at Miletus of wolves after his departing; the Qur’an asks the first Muslims whether they will turn back when their Messenger dies. Augustine, Tennyson, Shelley and Dickinson are here because grief is not only a religious matter. And the Preacher and the psalmist are here to ask whether mourning that refuses all rest can be asked of everyone.
questions: “It is expedient for you that I go away.” What do readings 18 to 21 say was given after the Ascension that could not be given before?
Paul warned of wolves entering after his departure, and the Qur’an of turning back. Why is the death of a founder the moment of greatest danger, and what in readings 11 to 13 was meant to meet it?
Paul lets his friends sorrow, but not “as others which have no hope”. Where in these letters is ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s own grief plain, and where does he lead others beyond it?
“Rest and comfort and pleasure are forbidden to us.” Set this beside “a time to mourn, and a time to dance”. How should a later generation, which did not know those days, read such sentences?
The gates of witnessing are closed. What do Thomas’s beatitude and Peter’s “we were eyewitnesses” each ask of those who come after?

outside.why: In his closing days he turns to the one gathering his papers. Paul to Timothy near the end: I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand.
“The Supreme Affliction was upon us.” Elisha, watching Elijah taken up, cries: My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof. And he saw him no more.
The once bright days “turned black as night”. How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! She weepeth sore in the night.
“Enemies within and enemies without” attacked after the ascension. Paul’s farewell at Miletus: after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you; also of your own selves shall men arise.
“This darkest night, the night of the Ascension.” By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.
The fire of separation “has uprooted the foundation” of life. Augustine after his friend died: my heart was utterly darkened, and whatever I looked upon was death.
Calamities and losses are hard to bear, because love torments the heart. At the grave of Lazarus: Jesus wept. Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him!
Paul would not have his friends sorrow “even as others which have no hope”. He does not forbid sorrow. What is the difference between grief with hope and grief without?
He set out to meet him and found he had ascended. Israel reaches the border of the land and its leader dies on the mountain, his grave unknown.
Hints of his departure in the prayers made the hearer sad. They all wept sore, sorrowing most of all for the words which he spake, that they should see his face no more.
The papers are gathered and entrusted. Moses, told that he is to be gathered to his people, is commanded to take Joshua and lay his hand upon him.
“They shall belong to thee.” The risen Jesus to Peter, three times: Feed my sheep.
As the end drew near, his talk turned to the Covenant. At the last supper: a new commandment I give unto you, that ye love one another.
He spoke well of distant friends at the last. Having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end.
Cholera broke out on the day of the Ascension, and a Christian neighbour said the talisman of ‘Akká was gone. The Gospel also marks a death with signs: the veil of the temple rent, the earth quaking.
The Light has set, “to shine everlastingly from the Abha Horizon”. Thy sun shall no more go down; for the Lord shall be thine everlasting light, and the days of thy mourning shall be ended.
Though the Daystar has passed to the invisible realm, its effulgence is before you. Shelley for Keats: he is not dead, he doth not sleep; he hath awakened from the dream of life.
He has ascended, yet his bounty is not cut off. It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you.
After his ascension “He did not deprive us”. I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever.
A cleric of ‘Akká tells of seeing him enter his room after his death. When the doors were shut, came Jesus and stood in the midst.
The women’s report from the tomb seemed to the apostles as idle tales, and they believed them not. How should such accounts be received, then and now?
Those who lived in his presence, “intoxicated with the wine of reunion”, see the sun set. The days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then shall they fast.
“Another tempest of trials now rages.” Simon, Simon, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not.
Some supposed the Cause would wane with his passing. The Qur’an to the first Muslims: Muhammad is but a messenger; will it be that, when he dieth, ye will turn back on your heels?
“The pillars of the world were shaken.” David’s lament: how are the mighty fallen in the midst of the battle!
“Gird up the loins of endeavor.” After the death of Moses, to Joshua: be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid.
A crown of sovereignty on the heads of the companions, as with the disciples of Jesus. Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
After the Ascension, embrace every tribulation. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you.
Bright day became darkest night, and for a purpose. Ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy.
“How can we take one moment’s rest?” The Preacher allots a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance. Must grief for such a loss refuse its season to end?
“Rest and comfort and pleasure are forbidden to us.” The psalm: so he giveth his beloved sleep. Is this a law for all, or the speech of one man’s love?
It becomes the faithful to rest not, but serve. Why stand ye gazing up into heaven?
Holy souls forgot this world after his passing. Tennyson, three years into mourning his friend: ’tis better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all.
“You were present … and witnessed.” We have not followed cunningly devised fables, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
Prove before the world that his passing caused no weakening. If this work be of men, it will come to nought: but if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it.
After the ascension “the divine lamp grew brighter”. Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.
“The gates of witnessing are closed, but you who perceived the days of meeting” must speak. Blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.
Emily Dickinson: parting is all we know of heaven, and all we need of hell. The guide moves from the second half of her line toward the first. What makes that movement honest?

shortfall: A few readings are short notes of fact (the renting of the mansion, the date, who was present) and were left without companions.
